To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the Presenilin1 gene is regulated by DNA methylation during neurodevelopment and neuro-degeneration in human and mouse brain; 2) DNA methylation of Presenilin1 is lower in Alzheimer’s disease patients than controls; 3) DNA methylation in Presenilin1 promoter region is associated with Presenilin1 mRNA expression in human and mouse brains.
the PSEN1 gene promoter methylation pattern in human and mouse brain is associated with PSEN1 gene expression and with AD progression.
1) PSEN1 DNA is methylated at both CpG and non CpG sites, and 2) this methylation is correlated with PSEN1 mRNA levels in both human and mice brains.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the epigenetic mechanisms that regulate the expression of genes involved in neurodegenerative disease.
the epigenetic regulation of PSEN1 expression.
the identification of novel epigenetic mechanisms in AD pathogenesis and the development of new biomarkers.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the PSEN1 gene is a target for epigenetic regulation and that the PSEN methylation pattern in peripheral blood could be useful as an early biomarker for AD.
the PSEN1 DNA CpG and non CpG methylation patterns are associated with gene expression and disease progression.
PSEN1 is a target of epigenetic regulation in human brain and blood and that its expression can be influenced by DNA methylation.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
DNA methylation of PSEN1 in blood may serve as a biomarker for early detection of AD.

PSEN1 is regulated by methylation in a gender and species specific manner, and that PSEN1 expression correlates with methylation in human brain and blood, suggesting that PSEN1 methyaltion may be a biomarker for disease.
PSEN1 gene expression in human brain is tightly associated with the methylation status of its 5ʹ flanking region, and the same holds true in mice, but only in females.
The main takeaway from our work is that
PSEN1 expression and methylation are tightly linked, and that this link is different in mice and humans.
PSEN1 methlylation in the brain and blood can be used to monitor disease progression in AD.
the PSEN1 gene undergoes dynamic changes in DNA methylation in the course of neurodevelopment, aging and disease progression.
